d.title: Lloyd's algorithm, and the objective it descends
d.caption: Each of the two steps can only **lower** the within-cluster sum of squares, so the loop converges — to a local minimum that depends on where the centres started, which is why `n_init` exists and why k-means++ spreads the initial centres. What the loop cannot change is the objective: k-means always seeks the partition minimising squared distance to a centre, so it finds round, similar-sized blobs whether or not the data has any.

d.title: Five rules for k, on data where the answer is known to be 4
d.caption: Four well-separated blobs. Every criterion agrees at k = 4 — inertia's elbow, the silhouette maximum, the Davies–Bouldin minimum, the Calinski–Harabasz maximum, and an **ARI of exactly 1.000** against the true labels. The gap statistic agrees too, at 1.424. That agreement is what a clear clustering looks like; the churn customers in §03 show what happens when the structure is not there, and the same five rules stop agreeing.

d.title: What k-means cannot find, whatever k you give it
d.caption: Each failure traces back to the objective. Minimising squared distance to a centre means clusters are convex and roughly equal in spread, so a crescent gets cut in half and a small dense cluster gets absorbed by a large diffuse one. On the churn customers there is no bend in the inertia curve at all — the data is a continuum, and k-means will still happily return any k you ask for.

cells.text: a big cluster absorbs a small one

d.title: Agglomerative clustering, and why the linkage is the whole decision
d.caption: Start with every row its own cluster and repeatedly merge the closest pair — but 'closest' has four definitions and they produce different shapes. **Single** linkage chains through noise and can snake a cluster across a dataset; **complete** forces compact balls; **Ward** minimises the variance increase and behaves most like k-means. The dendrogram is the deliverable: it lets you choose k after seeing the structure rather than before.

d.title: Six clustering families, by the shape each can find
d.caption: The first column is the question people ask and the second is the one that decides the answer. DBSCAN finds any shape **at one density**, which is exactly why HDBSCAN replaced it as the default: real data has clusters at several densities, and a single eps cannot describe them.

d.title: The BIC that collapsed, and why it was not structure
d.caption: BIC fell off a cliff at five components — from 2,502 to **−1,317** — and it means nothing. The discount column takes three values with 686 rows at zero, and two components had variance **0.0000** on it: a Gaussian concentrated on a point mass has unbounded density there, so the likelihood is arbitrarily large and BIC follows it down. A covariance floor of 0.1 removes the collapse and leaves a shallow, believable minimum at three.

d.title: HDBSCAN: one parameter instead of two, and noise as an answer
d.caption: DBSCAN's `eps` fixes one density for the whole dataset, so a parameter that finds the sparse cluster merges the dense ones. HDBSCAN builds the hierarchy over **all** densities and then extracts the clusters that persist longest, which removes `eps` entirely and leaves `min_cluster_size` — a number you can reason about, because it is 'how many rows make a group worth naming'.

nodes.sub: and it comes with a score

d.title: Five questions about a clustering, and the index for each
d.caption: The first row is the trap: on the two moons, k-means scored a silhouette of **0.487** and the true labelling scored **0.328** — so the internal index preferred the wrong answer, because it measures the geometry a convex method produces rather than the structure that is there.

d.title: Why agreement must be corrected for chance
d.caption: Two random partitions of the same rows agree substantially just by accident, and the raw Rand index reports that agreement as skill. ARI subtracts the expected value under random labelling, which is why it can go negative — and why a plain Rand index of 0.7 says almost nothing.
cells: each class sits in one cluster

d.title: Clustering on the right distance
d.caption: The metric **is** the model. Euclidean distance on raw TF-IDF measures document length as much as content, so cosine is the standard choice for text; two time series with the same shape offset by a day are far apart pointwise and identical under dynamic time warping. Changing the distance changes what 'similar' means, which changes every cluster — before any algorithm is chosen.

nodes.label: What does similar mean?
nodes.sub: answer this before choosing a method

d.title: Using clusters, and what each use demands of them
d.caption: The demands differ sharply. A segmentation shown to a marketing team needs to be **stable and nameable** and can afford to be statistically mediocre; a cluster id used as a model feature needs only to be reproducible at serving time, and must be fitted inside the fold like any other transform.

d.title: From 'maximise the variance' to an eigenproblem
d.caption: The derivation is short and it explains every property PCA has. Maximising the projected variance subject to a unit-length direction is a Lagrange problem whose stationary condition **is** the eigenvector equation — so the components are eigenvectors not by construction but by consequence, and their eigenvalues are the variances.

items.label: Centre the data
items.desc: without this the first component points at the mean

items.label: Ask for the unit direction of maximum variance
items.desc: maximise w'Cw subject to w'w = 1

items.label: Lagrange: Cw = lambda w
items.desc: the stationary condition is the eigenvector equation

items.label: So the variance along w is lambda
items.desc: the eigenvalue is the explained variance

items.label: Next direction, orthogonal to the first
items.desc: the second eigenvector, and so on

items.label: Equivalently, the SVD of the centred matrix
items.desc: which is how it is actually computed

d.title: Unscaled, PC1 *is* the tenure column
d.caption: On raw units the first component takes **80.2%** of the variance and its loadings are tenure 1.00 and everything else 0.00 — PCA has found the column measured in the largest numbers, which is not a discovery. Standardise and the picture changes completely: five components explain 35/21/20/19/5%, almost isotropic, and PC1 becomes 'plan tier', loading fee 0.71 and logins 0.71 together. Same data, same algorithm, different question answered.

d.title: The two claims PCA makes
d.caption: PCA asserts that the interesting directions are the **high-variance** ones and that the structure is **linear**. Nothing in the computation looks at the target, so a low-variance direction carrying all the signal is discarded without complaint — and no amount of components fixes a curved manifold.

d.title: The toolkit around PCA, and what each one buys
d.caption: They differ in what they preserve. PCA preserves global variance; a random projection preserves **pairwise distances** with no fitting at all; NMF gives additive parts, which is what makes its components readable as topics or spectra. Truncated SVD is the one to use on sparse text, because it works on X directly without centring — and centring a sparse matrix would fill in every zero.
cells: a cheap first squeeze; no fitting

d.title: PCA finds what varies; LDA finds what separates
d.caption: They can point in nearly opposite directions. If two classes differ along a low-variance axis, PCA throws that axis away and LDA keeps only it. LDA is supervised, which means it must be fitted inside the fold like any other label-using step.

d.title: What a t-SNE plot does and does not tell you
d.caption: It preserves neighbourhoods and negotiates away everything else. Cluster sizes here were stretched 4–14× **and in a different order**; between-cluster gaps correlate only 0.7 with the real ones; and pure Gaussian noise produced an embedding with a silhouette of 0.34. There is no `transform`, so a new point cannot be placed without re-running the whole embedding.
cells: they are neighbours in the input
the layout has no global meaning

d.title: The manifold family, and the one property that decides it
d.caption: Whether a method has a `transform` decides whether it can be part of a model at all. t-SNE has none — a new point cannot be placed without recomputing the entire embedding — so it is a tool for looking, never a preprocessing step. UMAP has one, which is the practical reason it displaced t-SNE in pipelines rather than in papers.

d.title: A grid of 25 points never found the peak; 25 random points nearly always did
d.caption: The target has a narrow peak on x₁ at 0.31 and a weak slope on x₂, with a maximum of 1.10. The 5×5 grid lands on x₁ ∈ {0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1} — never near 0.31 — and so returns **0.670, every single time**, with no variance to warn you. Twenty-five random points average 0.971. The probability argument explains it and does not depend on the dimension at all: if the good region is the top 5%, n draws all miss it with probability 0.95ⁿ.

d.title: Four searches on one SVM, and the budget that mattered more than the method
d.caption: Grid, random and TPE all land on 0.9644 — and random and TPE both reach it **within the first five trials**, so the sophistication bought nothing here; the space was simply not hard. Successive halving was fastest and finished worst, and the reason is in the note: the candidate that won on 250 rows was not the one that won on 2,000, which is the standing risk of judging on a subsample.

d.title: Why the tuned score is biased, and what nested CV costs
d.caption: Taking the best of n cross-validated scores is taking the maximum of n noisy numbers, and the maximum of noise is positive. The inner loop chooses; the outer loop measures a procedure that includes the choosing. There is no way to get both from one loop.

d.title: The measurement problem: 2.5% positives, and accuracy says 97.5%
d.caption: At a 2.5% base rate the do-nothing model is right 97.5% of the time, so accuracy cannot distinguish a useful model from a constant. PR-AUC can — its no-skill level **is** the prevalence, 0.025 — and so can recall at a fixed precision. This is the row to settle before any treatment is tried, because every treatment below will be judged by whichever metric you picked here.

d.title: SMOTE before the split, and the most seductive number in applied ML
d.caption: Every synthetic row is an interpolation of real minority rows, so when the split comes afterwards the training folds hold near-copies of the test folds' positives. The honest arrangement scores **worse than doing nothing at all** on this problem — which is the finding, not a disappointment.
rows: SMOTE on all rows, then CV

d.title: How SMOTE synthesises a row, and where that goes wrong
d.caption: A synthetic positive is a point on the line between a real positive and one of its k minority neighbours. Two consequences follow immediately: the new row carries **no information** that was not already in those two, and if the pair straddles a region of the majority class the interpolation lands inside it, manufacturing a positive where positives do not occur.

d.title: Six levers for imbalance, and which one actually moved
d.caption: The threshold is almost always the largest single gain — F1 went from 0.109 to 0.351 by moving it, with no change to the model. Most of the other treatments turn out to be a threshold change in disguise, which is why they should be compared against simply tuning the cut.

d.title: Four curve shapes, and what each one tells you to do next
d.caption: A learning curve answers 'would more data help' before you spend anything finding out. The first row is the one people act on wrongly: both lines low and together is **bias**, and more data does nothing — measured at 0.51 to 0.54 across a hundredfold increase in rows.

d.title: The course's own data, read by curve
d.caption: Two datasets, two diagnoses, and the action is opposite in each. The churn curve has both lines low and close and does **not** move with a hundredfold increase in rows — 0.51 to 0.54 — which is bias: the features are the ceiling. The boosting curve is still rising at the right edge, 0.775 to 0.917, which means data is the cheapest next step. Reading the curve first is what stops a month being spent on the wrong one.

d.title: Reading a curve in ten seconds
d.caption: Five questions in order, and the first one that answers yes tells you what to do. The last is worth stating explicitly: a validation curve whose two lines are flat across the whole range is telling you the dial does not matter, so stop searching it.

The dummy is first because it is the number everything else is reported against, and the cost column is there because a 0.002 gain that triples latency is not a gain.

d.title: Persistence, and the reload check that catches the version drift
d.caption: A pickle stores the object graph, not the behaviour — so the same file loaded against a different scikit-learn can predict differently, or fail to load at all. The golden-set check is the cheap guard: a handful of rows and their expected scores, compared on every reload, turning a silent behavioural change into a loud failure.

d.title: Four ways to persist a model, and what each trusts
d.caption: `joblib.load` **executes whatever the file tells it to** — a model artefact from an untrusted source is a remote-code-execution vector, and one from a trusted source that has been tampered with is the same thing. ONNX is a data-only graph, which is what makes it the format for crossing a trust boundary, and it was 40× faster in the request path here.
